claim: In most bacteria and eukaryotes, single-headed lipids self-assemble into flexible bilayer membranes.
source: In most bacteria and eukaryotes, single-headed lipids self-assemble into flexible bilayer membranes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about bacterial and eukaryotic membrane composition.

claim: Thermophilic archaea tend to possess bilayer lipids together with double-headed, monolayer spanning bolalipids.
source: By contrast, thermophilic archaea tend to possess bilayer lipids together with double-headed, monolayer spanning bolalipids, which are thought to enable cells to survive in harsh environments.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about archaeal membrane composition.

claim: Bolalipids are thought to enable cells to survive in harsh environments.
source: By contrast, thermophilic archaea tend to possess bilayer lipids together with double-headed, monolayer spanning bolalipids, which are thought to enable cells to survive in harsh environments.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis or speculation in the literature.

claim: Flexible bolalipids form membranes that resemble bilayer membranes because they are able to assume a U-shaped conformation.
source: We find that flexible bolalipids form membranes that resemble bilayer membranes because they are able to assume a U-shaped conformation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Rigid bolalipids, which resemble the bolalipids with cyclic groups found in thermophilic archaea, take on a straight conformation.
source: Conversely, rigid bolalipids, which resemble the bolalipids with cyclic groups found in thermophilic archaea, take on a straight conformation and form membranes that are stiff and prone to pore formation when they undergo changes in shape.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational simulations, with comparison to known archaeal lipid structures.

claim: Rigid bolalipids form membranes that are stiff and prone to pore formation when they undergo changes in shape.
source: Conversely, rigid bolalipids, which resemble the bolalipids with cyclic groups found in thermophilic archaea, take on a straight conformation and form membranes that are stiff and prone to pore formation when they undergo changes in shape.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational simulations.

claim: The inclusion of small amounts of bilayer lipids in a bolalipid membrane is enough to achieve fluid bolalipid membranes that are both stable and flexible.
source: Strikingly, however, the inclusion of small amounts of bilayer lipids in a bolalipid membrane is enough to achieve fluid bolalipid membranes that are both stable and flexible, resolving this trade-off.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational simulations.

claim: The bounding membrane must be sturdy and impermeable to the leakage of small charged molecules like ions, to allow the generation of an electrochemical gradient.
source: To perform its function, this bounding membrane must be sturdy and impermeable to the leakage of small charged molecules like ions, to allow the generation of an electrochemical gradient (Phillips et al., 2012), but also flexible enough to be remodelled during essential cellular processes like cell division and vesicle formation (McMahon and Gallop, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Phillips et al., 2012.

claim: The bounding membrane must be flexible enough to be remodelled during essential cellular processes like cell division and vesicle formation.
source: To perform its function, this bounding membrane must be sturdy and impermeable to the leakage of small charged molecules like ions, to allow the generation of an electrochemical gradient (Phillips et al., 2012), but also flexible enough to be remodelled during essential cellular processes like cell division and vesicle formation (McMahon and Gallop, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McMahon and Gallop, 2005.

claim: Two different generic membrane designs have evolved across the tree of life.
source: Interestingly, two different generic membrane designs have evolved across the tree of life to solve this problem (Gould, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gould, 2018.

claim: Bacterial and eukaryotic membranes possess fatty acid lipids that have a hydrophilic head group linked to hydrophobic tails via ester-linkages, which self-assemble into bilayer membranes.
source: Bacterial and eukaryotic membranes possess fatty acid lipids that have a hydrophilic head group linked to hydrophobic tails via ester-linkages, which self-assemble into bilayer membranes (Albers and Meyer, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Albers and Meyer, 2011.

claim: Archaeal membranes are constructed from branched isoprenoid lipids.
source: By contrast, archaeal membranes are constructed from branched isoprenoid lipids.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about archaeal membrane composition.

claim: Archaeal lipids can include cyclopentane rings and are attached via an ether linkage to one or two hydrophilic heads.
source: These can include cyclopentane rings and are attached via an ether linkage to one (e.g. archaeol, Figure 1A left) or two hydrophilic heads, leading them to be called bipolar lipids or simply bolalipids (e.g. caldarchaeol, Figure 1A right) (Albers and Meyer, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Albers and Meyer, 2011 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: For bolalipids, the two head groups at either end of the molecule are typically distinct.
source: For bolalipids, the two head groups at either end of the molecule are typically distinct (Figure 1A right) (Oger and Cario, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oger and Cario, 2013 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Archaea must keep their lipid membranes in a fluid state (homeoviscous adaptation).
source: Like for bacteria and eukaryotes, archaea must keep their lipid membranes in a fluid state (homeoviscous adaptation).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about membrane biology.

claim: Many archaea adapt to changes in their environment by tuning the lipid composition of their membranes: altering the ratio between bola- and bilayer lipids in their membranes.
source: Because of this, many archaea adapt to changes in their environment by tuning the lipid composition of their membranes: altering the ratio between bola- and bilayer lipids in their membranes (Tourte et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2019) and/or by changing the number of cyclopentane rings in their lipid tails, which are believed to make lipid molecules more rigid (Oger and Cario, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tourte et al., 2020 and Kim et al., 2019.

claim: Cyclopentane rings in lipid tails are believed to make lipid molecules more rigid.
source: Because of this, many archaea adapt to changes in their environment by tuning the lipid composition of their membranes: altering the ratio between bola- and bilayer lipids in their membranes (Tourte et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2019) and/or by changing the number of cyclopentane rings in their lipid tails, which are believed to make lipid molecules more rigid (Oger and Cario, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oger and Cario, 2013.

claim: Thermococcus kodakarensis increases its tetraether bolalipid ratio from around 50% to over 80% when the temperature of the environment increases from 60 to 85 °C.
source: For example, Thermococcus kodakarensis increases its tetraether bolalipid ratio from around 50% to over 80% when the temperature of the environment increases from 60 to 85 °C (Siliakus et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Siliakus et al., 2017.

claim: The cell membrane of Sulfolobus acidocaldarius can contain over 90% of bolalipids with up to eight cyclopentane rings at 70 °C and pH 2.5.
source: Along the same lines, the cell membrane of Sulfolobus acidocaldarius can contain over 90% of bolalipids with up to eight cyclopentane rings at 70 °C and pH 2.5 (Oger and Cario, 2013; Grogan, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Oger and Cario, 2013 and Grogan, 1989.

claim: In exceptional cases bacteria also synthesise bolalipids in response to high temperatures.
source: It is worth mentioning that in exceptional cases bacteria also synthesise bolalipids in response to high temperatures (Sahonero-Canavesi et al., 2022), highlighting that the study of bolalipid membranes is relevant not only for archaeal biology but also from a general membrane biophysics perspective.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sahonero-Canavesi et al., 2022.

claim: Archaeal lipids exhibit dense packing, high viscosity, and low porosity to small molecules like protons.
source: Besides temperature adaptation, archaeal lipids also exhibit dense packing, high viscosity, and low porosity to small molecules like protons (Siliakus et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Siliakus et al., 2017.

claim: The conformation of individual lipids in bolalipid membranes was studied at the water-air interface.
source: For instance, the conformation of individual lipids in bolalipid membranes was studied at the water-air interface (Bakowsky et al., 2000; Jeworrek et al., 2011) or using NMR experiments on lipid vesicles (Brownholland et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bakowsky et al., 2000 and Jeworrek et al., 2011.

claim: The conformation of individual lipids in bolalipid membranes was studied using NMR experiments on lipid vesicles.
source: For instance, the conformation of individual lipids in bolalipid membranes was studied at the water-air interface (Bakowsky et al., 2000; Jeworrek et al., 2011) or using NMR experiments on lipid vesicles (Brownholland et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brownholland et al., 2009.

claim: Studies suggested the existence of U-shaped lipid conformations in archaeal type membranes.
source: This suggested the existence of U-shaped lipid conformations in archaeal type membranes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the cited studies and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: In vitro reconstituted vesicles primarily composed of bolalipids can fuse with influenza virus particles at similar kinetic rates compared to bilayer vesicles.
source: Moreover, in vitro reconstituted vesicles primarily composed of bolalipids can fuse with influenza virus particles at similar kinetic rates compared to bilayer vesicles, further suggesting that bolalipids exist in U-shape allowing for membrane remodelling and fusion (Bhattacharya et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bhattacharya et al., 2024.

claim: Archaeal lipids derived membranes are exceptional in being stable up to temperatures of 80 °C.
source: Membrane properties like bending stiffness (Vitkova et al., 2020) or lipid phase (Chang, 1994) have also been measured in vesicles prepared from archaeal tetraether lipids to demonstrate that archaeal lipids derived membranes are exceptional in being stable up to temperatures of 80 °C (Chang, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chang, 1994.

claim: Experiments with lipid vesicles made from synthetic bilayer lipids that include cyclopentane rings showed that increasing the number of these rings increases membrane rigidity.
source: Moreover, experiments with lipid vesicles made from synthetic bilayer lipids that include cyclopentane rings, which naturally appear in lipids of extremophilic archaea, showed that increasing the number of these rings increases membrane rigidity (Batishchev et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Batishchev et al., 2020.

claim: The pore closure time in bolalipid membranes has been investigated using all-atom simulations.
source: Specifically, the pore closure time in bolalipid membranes, and the role of cyclopentane rings for membrane properties have been investigated using all-atom simulations, showing decreased lateral mobility, reduced permeability to water, and increased lipid packing (Galimzyanov et al., 2025; Chugunov et al., 2025; Pineda De Castro et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Galimzyanov et al., 2025, Chugunov et al., 2025, and Pineda De Castro et al., 2016.

claim: All-atom simulations showed decreased lateral mobility, reduced permeability to water, and increased lipid packing in bolalipid membranes.
source: Specifically, the pore closure time in bolalipid membranes, and the role of cyclopentane rings for membrane properties have been investigated using all-atom simulations, showing decreased lateral mobility, reduced permeability to water, and increased lipid packing (Galimzyanov et al., 2025; Chugunov et al., 2025; Pineda De Castro et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Galimzyanov et al., 2025, Chugunov et al., 2025, and Pineda De Castro et al., 2016.

claim: Using coarse-grained simulations, it was suggested that bolalipid membranes are thicker.
source: Moreover, using coarse-grained simulations, it was suggested that bolalipid membranes are thicker (Bulacu et al., 2012), exhibit a gel-to-liquid phase transition at higher temperature (Davis et al., 2007), and exhibit a reduced diffusivity (Dey and Saha, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bulacu et al., 2012.

claim: Bolalipid membranes exhibit a gel-to-liquid phase transition at higher temperature.
source: Moreover, using coarse-grained simulations, it was suggested that bolalipid membranes are thicker (Bulacu et al., 2012), exhibit a gel-to-liquid phase transition at higher temperature (Davis et al., 2007), and exhibit a reduced diffusivity (Dey and Saha, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Davis et al., 2007.

claim: Bolalipid membranes exhibit a reduced diffusivity.
source: Moreover, using coarse-grained simulations, it was suggested that bolalipid membranes are thicker (Bulacu et al., 2012), exhibit a gel-to-liquid phase transition at higher temperature (Davis et al., 2007), and exhibit a reduced diffusivity (Dey and Saha, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dey and Saha, 2020.

claim: The geometry of bolalipids is, through the effects of entropy alone, sufficient to shift the fluid phase of archaeal-type membranes so that they are stable at high temperatures.
source: Our coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations show that the geometry of bolalipids is, through the effects of entropy alone, sufficient to shift the fluid phase of archaeal-type membranes so that they are stable at high temperatures.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational simulations.

claim: Membranes assembled from bolalipids can have a much higher bending rigidity than bilayer-derived membranes.
source: We show that membranes assembled from bolalipids can have a much higher bending rigidity than bilayer-derived membranes, and are more likely to resist membrane shape changes as in fission.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational simulations.

claim: During membrane deformation, stress in bolalipid membranes is relieved by a small fraction of bolalipids taking up a U-shaped conformation.
source: During membrane deformation, stress in these bolalipid membranes is relieved by a small fraction of bolalipids taking up a U-shaped conformation, which renders them a mechanically switchable material.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational simulations.

claim: Without U-shaped bolalipids, stress leads to the formation of large pores.
source: Without these U-shaped bolalipids, stress leads to the formation of large pores.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational simulations.

claim: A mixture of bilayer and bolalipids generates membranes that are stable at high temperature, which become softer as the fraction of bilayer lipids increases.
source: However, when combined, a mixture of bilayer and bolalipids generates membranes that are stable at high temperature, which become softer as the fraction of bilayer lipids increases.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational simulations.

claim: The computational model extends the Cooke and Deserno model for bilayer membranes.
source: To study bolalipid membranes and compare them to bilayers, we extended the Cooke and Deserno model for bilayer membranes (Cooke and Deserno, 2005).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by a citation to Cooke and Deserno, 2005.

claim: A bolalipid molecule is modeled by joining two bilayer lipids.
source: To model a bolalipid molecule, we joined two bilayer lipids so that a lipid molecule is formed with a head bead (cyan) that is linked to four tail beads (crimson) which are again linked to another head bead (Figure 1C right).
evidence: This is a methodological description with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Both bilayer and bolalipid molecules self-assembled into membranes over a wide range of lipid interaction parameters.
source: For both bilayer and bolalipids, we found that membranes self-assembled over a wide range of lipid interaction parameters (Figure 1D, Figure 1—video 1, Appendix 1–Section 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations with reference to Figure 1D and video.

claim: Membranes made from flexible bolalipids are only slightly more rigid than bilayer membranes.
source: When we determined the bending rigidity of bolalipid membranes by measuring their response to thermal fluctuations, we found that membranes made from flexible bolalipids are only slightly more rigid than bilayer membranes.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations.

claim: Membranes made of stiff bolalipid molecules can exhibit stiffness that is more than an order of magnitude larger than that of bilayer lipids at the same membrane fluidity.
source: However, bolalipids in extremophilic archaea are not predicted to be fully flexible as they are expected to pack tighter due to a large number of cyclopentane rings in the lipid tails (Chong, 2010; Chong et al., 2012). Indeed, we found that membranes made of stiff bolalipid molecules can exhibit stiffness that is more than an order of magnitude larger than that of bilayer lipids at the same membrane fluidity.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations with supporting citations to Chong, 2010 and Chong et al., 2012.

claim: Membranes made from stiffer bolalipids showed a curvature-dependent bending modulus.
source: It is striking that membranes made from stiffer bolalipids showed a curvature-dependent bending modulus, which is a clear signature that bolalipid membranes exhibit hypoelastic behaviour during membrane reshaping.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations.

claim: The ratio of the Gaussian rigidity to the bending modulus for flexible bolalipid membranes is around −1/2.
source: Another marked difference between bilayer and flexible bolalipid membranes is the ratio of the Gaussian rigidity to the bending modulus. Instead of being around −1 as for bilayer membranes (Hu et al., 2012), it is around −1/2 and, therefore, only half of that of bilayer lipids.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations with a citation to Hu et al., 2012 for comparison.

claim: A small increase in the fraction of archaeal bilayer lipids should be sufficient to soften a bolalipid-rich membrane.
source: First, it predicts that a small increase in the fraction of archaeal bilayer lipids should be sufficient to soften a bolalipid-rich membrane.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: Membranes formed of a mixture of bilayer and bolalipids function as a composite liquid membrane that softens when adding bilayer lipids.
source: We found that membranes formed of a mixture of bilayer and bolalipids, similar to archaeal membranes, function as a composite liquid membrane that softens when adding bilayer lipids.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations.

claim: By enforcing curvature on bolalipid membranes, the fraction of U-shaped bolalipids increased around the cargo bud, especially in the outer membrane layer and hence softened the membrane.
source: We found that by enforcing curvature on bolalipid membranes, the fraction of U-shaped bolalipids increased around the cargo bud, especially in the outer membrane layer and hence softened the membrane.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations.

claim: Membrane pores form when the energetic cost required to change the bolalipid conformation to release bending stress is larger than the energetic cost of opening a lipid edge surrounding the pore.
source: We reasoned that pores form when the energetic cost required to change the bolalipid conformation to release bending stress is larger than the energetic cost of opening a lipid edge surrounding the pore.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation observations.

claim: The inclusion of small amounts of bilayer lipids in a bolalipid membrane can mend membrane pores.
source: As another mechanism to release curvature stress, we observed the formation of membrane pores, which could be mended by adding small amounts of bilayer lipids, similar to the mixture membranes that are found in archaea (Tourte et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations with a citation to Tourte et al., 2020.

claim: Enforcing membrane bending can soften bolalipid membranes locally by increasing the number of U-shapes, rendering the membrane a mechanically switchable material where large curvature decreases stiffness.
source: Our results suggest that enforcing membrane bending can soften bolalipid membranes locally by increasing the number of U-shapes, rendering the membrane a mechanically switchable material where large curvature decreases stiffness.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation findings.

claim: Archaeal membranes can balance opposing needs when adapting to extreme environmental conditions.
source: Taken together, our results show how membranes which are mixtures of bilayer and bolalipids maintain cell integrity at high temperatures, while also undergoing leak-free membrane bending. This suggests that archaeal membranes can balance opposing needs when adapting to extreme environmental conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation findings.

claim: The increase in membrane rigidity coincided with U-shaped bolalipids vanishing from the membrane.
source: Strikingly, the increase in membrane rigidity coincided with U-shaped bolalipids vanishing from the membrane (Figure 2B), which confirmed the hypothesis that straight bolalipids render lipid membranes rigid.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Bilayer and flexible bolalipids molecules form flexible membranes that prefer to bend rather than to tilt.
source: Since membrane bending and lipid tilting are two modes of membrane deformations that compete, we conclude that bilayer and flexible bolalipids molecules form flexible membranes that prefer to bend rather than to tilt, while bolalipids in straight configuration form rigid membranes that prefer to tilt rather than to bend.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation findings.

claim: Bolalipids in straight configuration form rigid membranes that prefer to tilt rather than to bend.
source: Since membrane bending and lipid tilting are two modes of membrane deformations that compete, we conclude that bilayer and flexible bolalipids molecules form flexible membranes that prefer to bend rather than to tilt, while bolalipids in straight configuration form rigid membranes that prefer to tilt rather than to bend.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation findings.

claim: Mixing only 10% bilayer lipids into the bolalipid membrane in gel state is enough to fluidize the membrane.
source: Interestingly, we found that mixing only 10% bilayer lipids into the bolalipid membrane in gel state is enough to fluidize the membrane (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: The bolalipid membrane can be substantially softened either through bolalipids acquiring the U-shaped conformation or through addition of bilayer-forming lipids.
source: Taken together, the bolalipid membrane can be substantially softened either through bolalipids acquiring the U-shaped conformation or through addition of bilayer-forming lipids.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation findings.

claim: Bolalipid membranes show marked hypoelastic behaviour as they soften during reshaping.
source: Hence, bolalipid membranes show marked hypoelastic behaviour as they soften during reshaping.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation findings.

claim: The membrane was able to curve by increasing the fraction of U-shaped bolalipids in the outer layer of the deformation.
source: Through analysing the bolalipid conformations, we found that the membrane was able to curve by increasing the fraction of U-shaped bolalipids in the outer layer of the deformation (Figure 4C, Appendix 1–Section 12).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: While large pores were not observed in the flat membrane, the diameter of membrane pores around the cargo was found to grow with the increase in bolalipid stiffness.
source: While large pores were not observed in the flat membrane, the diameter of membrane pores around the cargo was found to grow with the increase in bolalipid stiffness.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations.

claim: For relatively flexible bolalipids, U-shaped bolalipids provide the necessary area difference between the outer and inner layer of the membrane bud and thereby soften the membrane.
source: Hence, for relatively flexible bolalipids, U-shaped bolalipids provide the necessary area difference between the outer and inner layer of the membrane bud and thereby soften the membrane.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation findings.

claim: For stiff bolalipid molecules, membrane pores start to form to enable membrane curvature as U-shaped bolalipids become prohibited.
source: For stiff bolalipid molecules, however, membrane pores start to form to enable membrane curvature as U-shaped bolalipids become prohibited.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation findings.

claim: The onset energy sharply decreases with increasing amount of bilayer forming lipids, and plateaus for 50% bilayer head fraction.
source: We found that the onset energy sharply decreases with increasing amount of bilayer forming lipids, and plateaus for 50% bilayer head fraction, where it acquires similar values as in the case of fully-flexible bolalipids (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: For small bilayer fractions, U-shaped bolalipids localize almost exclusively on the outer layer of the bud.
source: For small bilayer fractions, U-shaped bolalipids localize almost exclusively on the outer layer of the bud (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: As the bilayer fraction increases, there is a steady reduction in the percentage of U-shaped bolalipids in the outer layer in favour of bilayer lipids.
source: As the bilayer fraction increases, there is a steady reduction in the percentage of U-shaped bolalipids in the outer layer in favour of bilayer lipids that take their role in supporting membrane curvature, with U-shaped bolalipids completely vanishing at high fractions of bilayer-forming lipids.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations.

claim: As the bilayer lipid fraction increases, the role of U-shaped bolalipids in making up the asymmetry between the outer and inner layer is taken over by bilayer lipids.
source: Taken together, as the bilayer lipid fraction increases, the role of U-shaped bolalipids in making up the asymmetry between the outer and inner layer is taken over by bilayer lipids.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation findings.

claim: The addition of bilayer lipids promotes the formation of U-shaped lipids, both in the flat membrane and even in the inner layer around the bud.
source: Curiously, the addition of bilayer lipids promotes the formation of U-shaped lipids, both in the flat membrane and even in the inner layer around the bud.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations.

claim: When more bilayer lipids are incorporated, the membrane is less densely packed and thus U-shaped bolalipids are promoted.
source: This is likely to be explained by the fact that when more bilayer lipids are incorporated, the membrane is less densely packed (Appendix 1—figure 12) and thus U-shaped bolalipids are promoted.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation observations with reference to Appendix figure.

claim: Nearly no pores were observed in the membrane bud in mixed membranes, even when there was only a very small fraction of bilayer-forming lipids.
source: Importantly, we observed nearly no pores in the membrane bud in mixed membranes, even when we only had a very small fraction of bilayer-forming lipids (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: As the bilayer fraction increased, very small pores were observed in the bud.
source: Only as the bilayer fraction increased, did we observe the formation of very small pores in the bud.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations.

claim: The pore formation in the flat mother membrane is likely promoted because the membrane becomes destabilized by the increasing proportion of bilayer lipids which are close to the gas phase.
source: The pore formation in the flat mother membrane is likely promoted because the membrane becomes destabilized by the increasing proportion of bilayer lipids which are close to the gas phase.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation observations.

claim: Bolalipids can bud porelessly when bilayer-forming lipids, which cause membrane softening, are included.
source: Taken together, bolalipids can bud porelessly when bilayer-forming lipids, which cause membrane softening, are included.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation findings.

claim: Doping a bolalipid membrane with a small fraction of bilayer lipids can relieve the trade-off, enabling membranes to be both stable under extreme conditions and to be remodelled without leaking.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate how doping a bolalipid membrane with a small fraction of bilayer lipids can relieve the trade-off, enabling membranes to be both stable under extreme conditions and to be remodelled without leaking.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation findings.

claim: The original theory of Helfrich, 1973 failed to describe the resulting height fluctuation spectrum of bolalipid membranes.
source: Interestingly, we found that the original theory of Helfrich, 1973 failed to describe the resulting height fluctuation spectrum.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations with a citation to Helfrich, 1973.

claim: The extended theory by Hamm and Kozlov, 2000, which also includes the energetic cost of lipid tilt, successfully captured bolalipid fluctuations.
source: However, the extended theory by Hamm and Kozlov, 2000, which also includes the energetic cost of lipid tilt, successfully captured bolalipid fluctuations (Appendix 1–Section 16).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations with a citation to Hamm and Kozlov, 2000.

claim: Previous coarse-grained simulations using the MARTINI force field showed that the ratio of straight to U-shaped bolalipids increased upon stiffening the linker between the lipid tails.
source: These results agree with the previous coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations using the MARTINI force field which showed that the ratio of straight to U-shaped bolalipids increased upon stiffening the linker between the lipid tails (Bulacu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bulacu et al., 2012.

claim: Previous coarse-grained simulations predicted that bolalipids spontaneously transition between the straight and U-shaped conformations.
source: While previous coarse-grained simulations predicted that bolalipids spontaneously transition between the straight and U-shaped conformations (Bulacu et al., 2012), how this happens in archaeal membranes and whether membrane proteins are involved in this conformational transition needs to be clarified in the future.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bulacu et al., 2012.

claim: Experimental studies suggest that archaeal membranes contain flippases and scramblases for the transitioning of bilayer lipids between membrane leaflets.
source: Experimental studies suggest that archaeal membranes contain flippases and scramblases for the transitioning of bilayer lipids between membrane leaflets (Makarova et al., 2015; Verchère et al., 2017), raising the possibility that similar proteins could also facilitate conformational transitions in bolalipids.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Makarova et al., 2015 and Verchère et al., 2017.

claim: It has been suggested that the viral fusion protein hemagglutinin could cause a transition from straight to U-shaped bolalipid conformation during the fusion of bolalipid vesicles with influenza viruses.
source: In addition, it has been suggested that the viral fusion protein hemagglutinin could cause a transition from straight to U-shaped bolalipid conformation during the fusion of bolalipid vesicles with influenza viruses (Bhattacharya et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bhattacharya et al., 2024.

claim: Previous atomistic simulations showed that the membrane rigidity was similar for membranes composed of bilayer lipids and flexible synthetic bolalipids.
source: This result is consistent with previous atomistic simulations, which showed that the membrane rigidity was similar for membranes composed of bilayer lipids and flexible synthetic bolalipids (Schroeder et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schroeder et al., 2016.

claim: A continuum theory predicted that the rigidity of membranes formed of triblock copolymers is 20% larger than that of diblock copolymers.
source: Moreover, the result is consistent with a continuum theory which predicted that the rigidity of membranes formed of triblock copolymers is 20% larger than that of diblock copolymers (Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2019.

claim: Colloidal membranes at macroscopic scales follow the standard Helfrich theory for bilayer membranes.
source: It has been found that colloidal membranes at these macroscopic scales follow the standard Helfrich theory for bilayer membranes (Barry and Dogic, 2010), with rigidity that is three orders of magnitude higher than those of lipid bilayers (Balchunas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barry and Dogic, 2010 and Balchunas et al., 2019.

claim: Previous experiments of mixture membranes of bilayer and bolalipids with cyclopentane rings suggested that the bending rigidity non-monotonically depends on the fraction of the membrane made up of bilayer lipids.
source: However, while in our simulations the bending rigidity monotonically decreases with bilayer fraction, previous experiments of mixture membranes of bilayer and bolalipids with cyclopentane rings suggested that the bending rigidity non-monotonically depends on the fraction of the membrane made up of bilayer lipids (Vitkova et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vitkova et al., 2020.

claim: Experiments reported that membranes consisting solely of bolalipids are more rigid than bilayer membranes and non-fluctuating.
source: The same experiments reported that membranes consisting solely of bolalipids are more rigid than bilayer membranes and non-fluctuating, which is in agreement with our high bending modulus simulation results for near-pure bolalipid mixture membranes.
evidence: This is supported by reference to the same experiments (Vitkova et al., 2020) and comparison to simulation results.
